scope: Where the frame time actually goes, and the largest available win

accounting_ms_per_frame_median.reading: the geometry construction is 44 per cent of a frame, more than motion and clustering together; the earlier profiles attributed this to the rail profile (about 18 ms, 854 median/mean calls per construction), rail-pair refinement (about 14 ms), normal covariances (7.3 ms) and the ground plane fit (4.3 ms)

opportunity_measured.idea: the ground and rail estimators do not need the walls, ceiling, ducts or the neighbouring track: rail returns lie at the gauge lines and the bed across the walkable width. Restricting their input to a lateral band should cost nothing in fitted geometry and much less in time.

straight_recording.band_2_0_m: 10420 points, 18.2 ms (55.6 ms full), anchor counts equal but rail anchors differ by up to 0.57 m - 2.0 m cuts into the neighbouring track's rail
straight_recording.band_2_5_m: rail anchors BIT-IDENTICAL (max |dx| 0.0000, max |dy| 0.0000), ground anchors and plane identical, rail head height identical

curved_recording.band_2_5_m_sensor_frame: 29516 points, 36.5 -> 29.0 ms, ground anchors and plane identical, but one rail anchor moves 0.0358 m laterally

opportunity_measured.conclusion: a lateral band around the CORRIDOR, not around the sensor axis, is the version to implement: on the straight recording it reproduces the geometry exactly, and the curved recording shows why the sensor-frame band is not enough - the corridor leaves the axis on a curve, so a sensor-frame band changes which rail returns are seen

not_shipped: no code change: the band as tested changes a rail anchor by 3.6 cm on the curve, which is decision-affecting, so it needs the corridor-aware form and the full gate (1460-frame panel identity, both recordings' statuses, labelled obstacle preserved) before it can be committed

also_measured.chain_filter_row_matching: np.unique over the cloud alone (72568 rows) is 21.9 ms, and the committed chain filter stacks every object's support on top of the cloud before that call - worth replacing with the object metadata it already carries (centre, extent, bbox), which gives the same cross-section position without the stack
also_measured.association: 10.1 ms for the assignment over roughly 200 tracks x 200 objects; the field's standard fix is a spatial gate that decomposes the assignment into small independent subproblems

corrected_attribution.what_i_expected: the rail window loop and its 2-D np.unique were the cost, so a lateral band would cut it

what_measurement_shows.rail_eligible_points: 1443 of 72590 - the rail estimator already works on a tiny subset
what_measurement_shows.rail_window_loop: sort 0.02 ms, searchsorted across 17 windows 0.07 ms, 2-D np.unique 1.11 ms in total
what_measurement_shows.so_the_loop_is_not_the_cost: the band hypothesis is disproved: there is nothing meaningful to save by banding the rail estimator's input, and the 4 m band it uses is deliberate - it must see both tracks to choose the correct rail pair, which is why 2.5 m moved an anchor 3.6 cm on the curve

where_the_55_ms_actually_is.normal_statistics / normal_covariances: about 7.3 ms - and it feeds background.py, whose surface normals drive background removal, so it is decision-relevant and cannot simply be moved off the critical path
where_the_55_ms_actually_is.still_unattributed: roughly 28 ms of the constructor, most plausibly the TunnelBackground construction over all 72590 points, which the next profile must measure directly

corrected_attribution.next_step: profile TunnelBackground's construction; that is where the remaining geometry time is, and unlike the rail band it has not been ruled out

background_model_is_the_frame.measured: TunnelBackground construction is 40.3 ms on 72590 points, 33 per cent of a 123 ms frame - larger than the geometry estimators it sits inside
background_model_is_the_frame.structure: about 22 overlapping windows of 30 m with 3 planes each and 120 RANSAC iterations per plane, rebuilt from scratch on every frame
background_model_is_the_frame.no_duplicate_to_share: its normals come from its own voxelised sample (voxel 0.1 m) with its own radius and neighbour parameters, so they are not the same computation as TrackGeometry's and cannot simply be handed over
background_model_is_the_frame.why_it_can_be_cached: the surfaces it models - lining, walls, ducts - do not change between consecutive frames at the same station. Both the field's background-modelling practice and the earlier research on this problem describe the same design: a PERSISTENT INFRASTRUCTURE MAP updated slowly, kept separate from SHORT-TERM OCCUPANCY
background_model_is_the_frame.the_safe_form: cache the fitted planes for stations BEHIND the train in world coordinates and re-project them into the current sensor frame, fitting fresh planes only ahead. Nothing ahead is ever cached before it has been observed, which removes the known failure mode of a stationary obstacle being absorbed into the background - the exact risk the level-crossing background-modelling work warns about
background_model_is_the_frame.expected_win: most of the 40 ms after the first frames of a run, i.e. the largest single runtime win available in this system
background_model_is_the_frame.verification_plan: plane caches change the model by design, so the panel cannot be byte-identical; the gate is the panel's metrics (event recall 0.8021, matched IoU 0.8223, zero negative episodes), both recordings' statuses with the labelled obstacle preserved 52 of 52, and a measured frame time before and after
background_model_is_the_frame.not_attempted: no code written: the cache is a real feature, and a half-verified version of it would be worse than none
